newsitem.title: USA: Democratic House win would not hurt bonds - experts.
newsitem.headline: Democratic House win would not hurt bonds - experts.

text.p: The chance that the Democrats could win one house of Congress in addition to the Presidency on Tuesday is said to have prompted some bond market selling late last week.

But political and fiscal policy experts say who wins control of the U.S. House of Representatives might make little difference to prospects for a balanced federal budget and therefore to the bond market.
Bond investors, whose fears often are reflected in higher interest rates, form a strong constituency for low inflation and fiscal restraint.
On the eve of the November 5 election, political scientists call the race to be the dominant political party in the House too close to call.

But whether Democrats regain the House or Republicans retain a majority, the political winds have shifted to favor fiscal prudence and even a balanced budget, experts said. Whatever their party affiliation, politicians will have to sail accordingly.

"From the point of view of the bond market, it doesn't make a great deal of difference whether the Democrats take Congress or not," said Robert Shapiro, vice president of the Progressive Policy Institute, the think-tank for the Democratic Leadership Council.

"The President and the House and Senate Democratic leadership are committed to a balanced budget," said Shapiro. "I find it very hard to imagine circumstances under which that commitment could slip without significant political cost."
Pressure for deficit reduction will "still be there," agreed Brookings Institute Senior Fellow Charles Schultz.

Schultz, who served as Chairman of the Council of Economic Advisors during the Carter Administration, even argued that a narrow Democratic majority might be the most effective prescription for budget reduction.
A very narrow Democratic majority could entail responsibility, said Schultz. "You couldn't just blame (current House Speaker) Newt Gingrich for everything."
Martha Phillips, executive director of the Concord Coalition, a public policy group advocating a balanced budget and the reining in of entitlement programs, agreed.

Phillips, the Republican staff director of the House Budget Committee from 1986 to 1992, said Congressional Democrats have always "used every tool at their disposal" to defeat a balanced-budget Constitutional amendment, asserting that the budget could be balanced without one.

When the Democrats held the Congress and the Republicans occupied the White House, the Democrats would proclaim that they were ready to balance the budget -- if only the President would exercise his leadership.
Meanwhile, said Phillips, the Republican president would claim that he was ready to balance the budget if it were not for "the mean old Congress" standing in his way.
If Democrats held both the Presidency and the House, they would have "a chance to show they really can balance the budget without the Constitutional amendment," said Phillips.
A Democratic majority would not be a big one so Clinton could work with a centrist coalition of so-called Blue Dog Democrats and moderate Republicans, said Schultz.

While Democrats "have a bigger propensity to spare some elements of spending than Republicans do, the other side is that with the responsibility of leadership, they can't just thumb their noses at fiscal responsibility," he said.
Phillips said even Democratic rhetoric now pays some homage to the goal of balancing the budget.

"They have shown some restraint in not calling for expansions of spending," she said. "Whenever they talk about some new program, they inject a note of caution, saying that we have to figure out a way to pay for it," she said.
Democratic strategists say one strategy that would be devastating for the bond market is the 15 percent tax cut proposed by Republican Presidential candidate Bob Dole.
"A tax cut would throw a balanced budget out the window," said Shapiro. Dole supporters on Wall Street say the former Senator would pay for the tax cut with spending cuts.

But Wall Street also reads the public opinion polls and President Clinton's wide lead in those tallies has kept the bond market from worrying about the impact of a prospective Dole tax cut on the U.S. budget.

If it makes little real difference to the bond market whether the Democrats capture a small majority in the House -- the prospect of Democrats achieving a majority in the Senate seems relatively remote, experts say -- an intriguing question is whether it even matters much to President Clinton.
One scholar contended that Clinton might even prefer a narrow Republican majority in the House.

"What needs to be stressed is Clinton's apparent ambivalence about a Democratic victory," said Pulitzer Prize-winning historian David Garrow. "Do Clinton and Gore really want to end up with a House where Dick Gephardt (D-Mo.) and David Bonior (D-Mich.) are empowered? Because these guys are more liberal than they are. Or would they prefer a 219-216 split (between Republicans and Democrats, respectively)?"
Garrow argued that if the House goes Democratic, liberals like Charles Rangel (D-N.Y.), David Bonior and John Dingell (D-Mich.) will be dramatically "energized."

But if Gingrich were to keep the House leadership -- but as head of a much diminished Republican majority -- "no one will have pizazz," Garrow said. "Everyone will be underwhelmed. And if Clinton wants to play King of the Hill, it's better for him if Congress is a little shrunken."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
